## Joseph Spencer’s *For Zion*

<div class="book-intro">
<div class="book-cover">
<img src="for-zion-cover.jpg" alt="Cover of For Zion: A Mormon Theology of Hope by Joseph M. Spencer">
</div>
<div class="book-copy">
<span class="label">A Mormon Theology of Hope · 2014</span>
<h3>What does it mean to hope for Zion?</h3>
<p>Spencer reads Romans 4,5, & 8 to clarify Christian hope, then connects that account to Restoration scripture and the work of consecration.</p>
<p>The book asks how hope for a transformed future changes our responsibility now.</p>
</div>
</div>

::: {.source-note}
Joseph M. Spencer, *For Zion: A Mormon Theology of Hope* (Greg Kofford Books, 2014). Book description and cover: [Greg Kofford Books](https://gregkofford.com/collections/scripture/products/for-zion-a-mormon-theology-of-hope).
:::

## Romans 4:18 centers the conversation

<div class="lede">In Romans 4, Paul uses Abraham to show how faith rests on God’s promise when the present offers no reason for hope.</div>

<div class="scripture-compare">
<div>
<span class="label">King James Version</span>
<blockquote>“Who against hope believed in hope, that he might become the father of many nations, according to that which was spoken, So shall thy seed be.”</blockquote>
</div>
<div>
<span class="label">New Living Translation</span>
<blockquote>“Even when there was no reason for hope, Abraham kept hoping, believing that he would become the father of many nations. For God had said to him, ‘That’s how many descendants you will have!’”</blockquote>
</div>
</div>

<div class="big-claim">Hopeless but hoping, Abraham believed he would become “the father of many nations.”
</div>

<div class="phrase-translation"><span class="label">Joseph Spencer’s phrase translation</span></div>

::: {.notes}
Romans 4 reads Genesis 15 as an account of the faith that God reckons as righteousness.

> Hopeless but hoping, Abraham believed he would become “the father of many nations.”

The promise looked impossible. Abraham and Sarah could not produce the promised future through their own capacities.

Hope gave faith consistency. Abraham trusted God to fulfill the promise when the present offered no visible path.

For Paul, hope gives faith its strength.

Source: Joseph M. Spencer, *For Zion* (Salt Lake City: Greg Kofford Books, 2014), ch. 2, “Faith and Hope.”
:::

## Hope for my future or God's

<div class="compare">
<div>
<span class="label">Everyday hope</span>
<h3>My desired future</h3>
<p>I expect my plans or claims to succeed. The future stays organized around what I want.</p>
</div>
<div>
<span class="label">Theological hope</span>
<h3>God's promised future</h3>
<p>I release control over the outcome and trust God’s promise to be fulfilled in God’s way.</p>
</div>
</div>

<div class="big-claim">Faith redirects hope from self-importance toward trust in God.</div>

::: {.source-note}
Spencer, *For Zion*, ch. 2, “Faith and Hope.”
:::

## Hope begins at the limit

<div class="metric-layout">
<div>
<div class="metric-word">No way</div>
<div class="metric-label">within the present order</div>
</div>
<div class="metric-copy">
<span class="label">Objective hopelessness</span>
<h3>The obstacle is more than my ingenuity</h3>
<p>Genuine hope faces the situation without pretending that another technique or burst of effort will solve it.</p>
</div>
</div>

<div class="big-claim">Hope faces reality without treating it as the final measure of possibility.</div>

::: {.source-note}
Spencer, *For Zion*, ch. 2, “Faith and Hope.”
:::

## Love turns hope into shared work {.love-slide}

<div class="love-content">
<blockquote class="love-quote">
<p>“hope becomes, instead, a <strong>loving confidence</strong> in the work to be accomplished by <strong>all who share in God’s vision.</strong>”</p>
</blockquote>

<p class="love-application">For education: hope takes shape in work we share with learners and educators.</p>
</div>

<div class="love-scripture">
<span class="label">Romans 5:3–5 · King James Version</span>
<p><sup>3</sup> And not only so, but we glory in tribulations also: knowing that tribulation worketh patience; <sup>4</sup> And patience, experience; and experience, hope:</p>
<p><sup>5</sup> And <strong>hope maketh not ashamed;</strong> because <strong>the love of God</strong> is shed abroad in our hearts by the Holy Ghost which is given unto us.</p>
</div>

::: {.source-note .love-source}
Joseph M. Spencer, *For Zion*, ch. 3, “Hope and Love.”
:::

::: {.notes}
The previous slide names the limit of the present order. Chapter 3 moves from that limit to the work of transformation: God enlists faithful, hopeful people in making a different world possible.

Paul’s argument moves from Abraham in Romans 4 to the connection between faith, hope, and love in Romans 5. In Romans 5:5, hope does not put us to shame because God’s love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit.

Spencer argues that hope grows through the difficulties of this work. Love then transforms it into partnership with God, an ongoing conversation about the world’s possibilities. This keeps hope from becoming confidence in our own independent abilities.

For educators, this account invites an analogy: learning can be shared work with students, sustained by conversation about what becomes possible together. This is an application of Spencer’s account to education, rather than a claim that technological change fulfills God’s promise.

Scripture source: [Romans 5:3–5, KJV](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Romans+5%3A3-5&version=KJV).

Source: Joseph M. Spencer, *For Zion: A Mormon Theology of Hope* (Greg Kofford Books, 2014), ch. 3, “Hope and Love.”
:::

## Hope and the future of learning {.transition-slide background-color="#244138"}

<div class="transition-question">
How can Spencer’s account of hope reshape education’s response to AI?
</div>

<div class="transition-subtitle">
What becomes possible when restoring the older order stops being the goal?
</div>

## Hope opens a different future {.ai-slide background-color="#e8f0eb"}

<div class="world-claim">The world can<br>become otherwise.</div>

<div class="world-copy">
<p>Despair accepts the world’s limits and gives up. Desperation searches for a hidden route inside them.</p>
<p>Hope trusts that learning can take a new form beyond the present “scheme of things.”</p>
</div>

## AI exposes the old order {.ai-slide background-color="#e8f0eb"}

<div class="lede">AI made several old assumptions in education harder to defend.</div>

<div class="three-ways">
<div>
<span class="label">Evidence</span>
<h3>The take-home essay</h3>
<p>A finished product no longer establishes who did the thinking.</p>
</div>
<div>
<span class="label">Effort</span>
<h3>Homework completion</h3>
<p>Submitted work gives weaker evidence of the effort behind it.</p>
</div>
<div>
<span class="label">Authority</span>
<h3>The information gatekeeper</h3>
<p>Teachers no longer control access to explanations and examples.</p>
</div>
</div>

<div class="big-claim">AI did not create every weakness in education. It made the old order visible.</div>

## Desperation seeks a procedure to maintain the old order {.ai-slide background-color="#e8f0eb"}

<div class="lede">Opposing positions can share the same commitment to restoring control.</div>

<div class="compare">
<div>
<span class="label">Frantic crackdown</span>
<h3>Find the perfect <span class="phrase-highlight">defense</span></h3>
<p>Detectors and lockdown browsers promise to restore the old evidence of learning.</p>
</div>
<div>
<span class="label">Frantic adoption</span>
<h3>Find the perfect <span class="phrase-highlight">integration</span></h3>
<p>Tools and frameworks promise control while leaving old purposes and structures untouched.</p>
</div>
</div>

<div class="big-claim spacious-claim">Both positions can become a <span class="phrase-highlight">hunt</span> for a procedure that will <span class="phrase-highlight">save the existing system</span>.</div>

## Despair names what the old order can't sustain {.ai-slide background-color="#e8f0eb"}

<div class="order-layout">
<div>
<span class="order-number">01</span>
<span class="label">Admission</span>
<h3>The old evidence cannot return</h3>
<p>A take-home essay cannot reliably verify who did the thinking. No detector can recreate the former assumption of authorship.</p>
</div>
<div>
<span class="order-number">02</span>
<span class="label">Opening</span>
<h3>That admission opens hope</h3>
<p>Once restoring stops being the goal, educators can redesign learning around better evidence and deeper relationships.</p>
</div>
</div>

<div class="big-claim">Hope begins where restoring ends.</div>

## Faith anchors educational purpose {.ai-slide background-color="#e8f0eb"}

<div class="scripture-block">

> “Seek learning, even by study and also by faith.” Doctrine and Covenants 88:118

</div>

<div class="split-idea">
<div>
<span class="label">Faith transforms hope</span>
<h3>Purpose guides our response to AI</h3>
<p>Education forms persons rather than producing assignments. Faith keeps hope oriented toward that purpose and gives us a measure for judging technology.</p>
</div>
<div>
<span class="label">Hope strengthens faith</span>
<h3>Purpose becomes a possible future</h3>
<p>Hope turns belief in education’s purpose into trust that learning can take new forms without losing what matters most.</p>
</div>
</div>

<div class="big-claim">Faith keeps hope about learning anchored in purpose.</div>

## AI can refocus LOVE in education {.ai-slide .love-ai-slide background-color="#e8f0eb"}

::: {.love-thesis}
> AI serves learning when it deepens the work educators and learners share.
:::

<div class="three-ways">
<div>
<span class="label">Dialogue</span>
<h3>Explore possibilities together</h3>
<p>Teachers and students question AI’s answers and consider what those answers miss.</p>
</div>
<div>
<span class="label">Oral defense</span>
<h3>Students explain choices</h3>
<p>Students explain how they used AI and give reasons for accepting or revising its suggestions.</p>
</div>
<div>
<span class="label">Apprenticeship</span>
<h3>Work develops in community</h3>
<p>Educators work alongside learners as they use AI, offering feedback and practicing judgment together.</p>
</div>
</div>

::: {.love-evidence}
> “Love [is] more than a mere emotion; it is a way of **working together to change the world**.”

> “Love is a consistently attentive way of living in which one is overwhelmed with happiness at realizing that **two different experiences can be shared** [in an] unending joint journey.”
:::

::: {.source-note}
Spencer, *For Zion*, ch. 3, “Hope and Love.” Educational application.
:::

::: {.notes}
Chapter 3 describes love as working together to change the world and as an ongoing conversation about the world’s possibilities. Hope becomes a loving confidence in work shared by those who participate in God’s vision.

Applied to education, this directs our response to AI toward shared learning. Dialogue, oral defense, and apprenticeship are established practices through which teachers and students can undertake that work together.

In dialogue, a generated answer becomes material for inquiry: What does it help us see? What does it overlook? In an oral defense, students explain their choices and evaluate suggestions with others. In apprenticeship, a teacher accompanies the learner’s process and develops judgment through feedback.

The educational examples are our application of Spencer’s theology. His chapter addresses partnership with God, rather than AI. The preceding slide establishes the educational purposes that guide this work.

Source: Joseph M. Spencer, *For Zion*, ch. 3, “Hope and Love”; highlighted passages in chapters/ch3/IMG_0385.PNG and IMG_0386.PNG.
:::
